title: Orphaned volume attach loop - incident notes and runbook changes
body:
Summary:

On 2025-11-02 09:18 UTC we observed a spike in API server latency followed by a wave of pending pods in several clusters (prod-us-west-2 and prod-eu-west-1). Root cause traces back to a CSI plugin regresssion that entered an attach-detach retry loop, producing thousands of attach/detach requests per minute. The attach storms overloaded the kube-controller-manager attach-detach controller and contributed to heavy etcd write load and increased kubelet CPU on a subset of nodes (due to repeated attach/detach calls and mount retries). Symptoms included: scheduler backpressure (many pods pending with attach/detach errors), node-reported DiskPressure on some nodes (stale mounts), and transient provisioning failures for stateful workloads.

Timeline (UTC):
- 09:15 - first pager: elevated API server request latency (99th percentile) alerted by alerting rule api-server.latency.
- 09:17 - SRE oncall (Riley) noted 100+ pods Pending with reason: AttachVolume.AttachVolume failed for several PVCs across clusters.
- 09:20 - Observed rapid increase in metrics: attachdetach_controller_ops/sec and number of AttachVolume events in kube-controller-manager logs.
- 09:25 - Identified repeated CSI logs on nodes: csi-driver: "Attach failed: attach request timed out, retrying" with monotonically increasing attempts.
- 09:30 - Began mitigation: rate-limit attach-detach controller by setting feature gate flags temporarily and scaled kube-controller-manager horizontally where allowed.
- 09:40 - Scoped affected nodes and patched CSI sidecar to v1.2.5 (rollback of v1.3.0), which stopped new attach storms.
- 09:55 - Gradual recovery as attach requests subsided; scheduler cleared backlog over next 40 minutes.

Key logs / evidence (excerpts):
- kube-controller-manager: "I1102 09:19:12.345 AttachVolume operation failed for volume pvc-abc: rpc error: code = DeadlineExceeded desc = context deadline exceeded"
- node csi-driver: "attach called for volume pvc-abc, attempt 42"
- etcd: leader write latency spike and increased txn/sec correlating with attach events (09:17-09:35)

Initial hypothesis and root cause analysis:
- The immediate cause was a regression in the CSI attach/detach controller introduced in v1.3.0 of our in-house csi-block-driver. The new retry logic removed exponential backoff under certain RPC error codes leading to rapid retrying.
- The rapid retries increased write rate to kube-controller-manager and etcd (object updates, status updates for VolumeAttachments), saturating API server resources and increasing scheduling latency.
- Some nodes accumulated stale mounts because detach completed on control-plane side but kubelet failed to clean up mounts quickly under CPU pressure, leading to DiskPressure conditions and further pod evictions.

Mitigations performed (ordered):
1) Short-term (first 30–60 minutes):
   - Scaled kube-controller-manager replicas where cluster config allowed (eks-managed cluster had limited scaling; self-managed clusters scaled +2).
   - Pinned CSI driver to previous stable version (rollback v1.3.0 -> v1.2.5) in affected clusters using rolling update with maxUnavailable=1.
   - Temporarily paused automated cronworkload that was triggering many mount-heavy jobs in prod (data-migration job), to reduce pressure on attach subsystem.
   - On two overloaded nodes we cordoned and drained replicas to offload mount cleanup and allow kubelet restart without risk to availability.

2) Medium-term (same day):
   - Increased Prometheus alerting thresholds to avoid noise for AttachVolume transient failures but added a dedicated alert for "attach-detach-op-rate" > 500/min for > 5m.
   - Backed off CSI attach/detach controller concurrency by setting controller flag --concurrent-operations=5 (was 50) on a temporary basis where safe.

3) Long-term (post-incident):
   - Reverted problematic retry semantics in csi-block-driver and added automated unit tests to exercise backoff behavior under transient RPC failures.
   - Added rate-limiting circuit-breaker in our attach-detach controller to avoid tight retry loops.
   - Improved monitoring: instrumented volumeattachment churn (unique volume attachments per minute) and added a Grafana dashboard that correlates AttachVolume ops, etcd txn/sec, and api-server latency.

Why this escaped pre-prod tests:
- The regression depended on a specific failure code path from our cloud provider's attach RPC that only surfaces under certain timing/latency windows which we did not simulate in CI. Our staging clusters have smaller volume churn patterns and didn’t trigger the loop during the rollout.

Open action items / follow-ups (owners):
- Aisha: finish postmortem doc and coordinate exec summary (deadline 2025-11-09).
- Marcus: backport the retry fix to 1.2.x and cut patched release; open PR and tag QA (RED-1123).
- Janelle: add an integration test that simulates transient attach RPC failures with no backoff to validate behavior across releases.
- Samir: instrument cluster-level quota for attach-detach operations (alert + soft-limit) and implement a controller-level circuit breaker by end of Q1 2026.
- SRE team: update runbook section Attach/Detach storm response with exact commands and safe rollback play (see below).

Runbook draft updates (append to cluster-ops runbook):
- Detect: query for large numbers of VolumeAttachment objects in state "attaching" more than X per minute: kubectl get volumeattachments --all-namespaces | wc -l; cross-check with prometheus metric attachdetach_ops/sec.
- Triage commands (fast):
  * kubectl -n kube-system logs deploy/csi-block-driver --since=10m | grep -i attach | tail -n 200\  
  * kubectl get pods -o wide --all-namespaces | grep Evicted\  
  * kubectl top nodes --use-protocol-buffers\  
  * kubectl get events --all-namespaces --field-selector reason=FailedAttachVolume
- Immediate mitigations (safe):
  * Pause any churn-inducing jobs (cronjobs, bulk provisioning)\  
  * Rollback CSI driver to last known-good (kubectl set image daemonset/csi-block-driver csi-block-driver=registry/...:v1.2.5)
  * Reduce controller concurrency: update deployment args --concurrent-operations=5 and restart controller pod to take effect.
- If API server is overloaded: scale controller-manager (if supported) and consider temporarily throttling controller loops via feature flags in the controller manager.

Post-incident monitoring additions:
- New alert: AttachDetachChurnHigh (attachdetach_ops/sec > 500 for 5m AND volumeattachments_churn_rate > threshold)
- Add dashboard panel: Attach ops vs etcd txn/sec vs api-server request latency over last 6 hours

Lessons learned (bullets):
- Tight retry loops in controllers can amplify transient RPC failures into cluster-wide failure modes through control-plane amplification.
- CI/integration tests must include failure-mode simulations (RPC timeouts, transient 5xx) for stateful subsystem drivers.
- Runbook needs a single-page "stop-the-bleed" checklist for attach-detach storms (who to notify, what to change, rollback commands).

Appendix (useful commands and snippets used during incident):
- count attaching VolumeAttachments: kubectl get volumeattachments -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}	{.status.attached}
{end}' | grep false | wc -l
- check controller logs for backoff behavior: kubectl -n kube-system logs deploy/kube-controller-manager --since=30m | grep -E "AttachVolume|DetachVolume" | sed -n '1,200p'
- safely cordon and drain (avoid mass evictions for stateful sets): kubectl cordon NODE && kubectl drain NODE --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --grace-period=300 --timeout=15m

Notes to self / oncall tips:
- If you see >200 attach attempts/minute, assume a bug in driver unless intentionally scaling provisioning.
- Prefer rolling rollback of CSI daemonset with maxUnavailable=1 to avoid causing mass detach events simultaneously.
- Keep slack thread pinned with summary and important timestamps so follow-ups are traceable.

Status: recovery verified 2025-11-02 10:45 UTC, full scheduler backlog cleared by 2025-11-02 11:30 UTC. Working on formal postmortem and patch rollout plan to all clusters.
